entries.title: The Lantern Accord
entries.text: In 1311 the prefects of the four houses met in the Great Hall and signed a single promise: the castle's corridors would stay lit all night, so that no student need walk in the dark. The original parchment hangs nowhere anyone can find it, which the prefects of the time considered a fine joke.

entries.title: Warden Fenwright's Rounds
entries.text: Isolde Fenwright was the first keeper of the castle lamps. She walked every floor twice a night with a long brass pole and gave each of the four hundred lamps a name. When she retired, she left a list of them, with notes on which ones sulked.

entries.title: Moonstone Oil
entries.text: The oldest lamps in the castle burn moonstone oil, pressed from moonstone dust and a little spring water. It burns slowly and gives a pale, steady light. Those who stand close say it smells faintly of rain.

entries.title: The Wandering Stairs
entries.text: The staircases first began to move in the winter of 1640, after the architect Aldous Merrow tried a charm to make them easier to climb. They became easier to climb, and also impossible to predict. They move most at dusk, when the castle settles for the night.

entries.title: The Steadfast Flight
entries.text: Of all the castle's stairs, one flight has never moved at all. Students call it the Steadfast Flight. Some say Merrow's charm simply missed it; others insist it heard the charm coming and refused.

entries.title: Merrow's Apologies
entries.text: Aldous Merrow spent the rest of his life writing letters of apology to the house prefects about the stairs. Forty-one of them survive. The later letters are shorter, and the last one reads, in full: Still sorry.

entries.title: The First Castle Owls
entries.text: Before there was any Owl Loft, a gamekeeper named Bram Hollins raised the castle's first owls in the West Tower. He fed them from his own supper and taught them the way to the village by walking it himself, with the owls riding on his hat.

entries.title: Old Tamsin
entries.text: The oldest owl on record was a grey barn owl called Old Tamsin. She carried the post for forty years without losing a single letter. She is said to have preferred toast crusts to mice, and to have bitten only those who deserved it.

entries.title: The Owl Exchange
entries.text: The Owl Exchange in the Entrance Hall was founded in 1762 so that students could trade without leaving the castle. The first trades on record were three quills for a pair of warm socks, in the middle of a very cold January.

entries.title: The Four Long Tables
entries.text: The four long tables of the Great Hall were cut from a single oak that fell in a storm in the forest. The carpenters split the trunk four ways so that no house would have the better wood. Students have been arguing about it ever since.

entries.title: The Founders' Oak
entries.text: Where the great oak once stood, a sapling was planted the following spring. It is now old enough to have a hollow, which new students are told contains a secret. The secret is mostly acorns.

entries.title: Sand from Four Shores
entries.text: The hourglasses that keep the house points were first filled with sand gathered from four different shores, one chosen by each house. Over the centuries the sand has been charmed to its house colours, but the grains are still said to be the same.

entries.title: The First House Cup
entries.text: The first House Cup was a dented pewter tankard, awarded to the house that had earned the most points in a single week. Its winners drank warm milk from it at the feast. The tankard was retired after someone tried to brew in it.

entries.title: The Portrait Guardians
entries.text: The common rooms were once closed by ordinary doors with ordinary keys. The keys kept vanishing, so the houses asked the castle's portraits to keep watch instead. The portraits agreed, on condition that they were allowed to judge the passwords.

entries.title: The Painter Ottoline Vask
entries.text: Ottoline Vask painted more than three hundred portraits for the castle. Scholars believe at least forty of them are of Ottoline herself in different hats. She never confirmed it, and the portraits will not say.

entries.title: The Kitchen Bells
entries.text: Below the Great Hall hangs a row of small bells, one for every table that has ever stood above. When a plate is empty for too long, its bell rings by itself. Nobody has ever found out who first charmed them.

entries.title: The Lake Mist
entries.text: On a few autumn mornings each year, mist rises from the lake in the shape of the castle, towers and all, and drifts slowly towards the hills. Those who see it are said to have good fortune with their letters for the rest of the week.

entries.title: The Corridor of Echoes
entries.text: On the seventh floor there is a stretch of corridor where footsteps echo a moment late, as if someone were following a step behind. Prefects on their rounds learned to stop suddenly. The echo learned to stop too.

entries.title: Lightning on the Tower
entries.text: The roof of the Astronomy Tower has been rebuilt three times after lightning strikes. The third rebuilding left it open to the sky altogether, which the astronomers of the day declared a great improvement.

entries.title: Why Divination Has a Ladder
entries.text: The Divination room is reached by a narrow stair and a ladder because, the story goes, the castle's ordinary stairs refused to go anywhere so unpredictable. The ladder had no opinion and was hired at once.

entries.title: The Charms Tiers
entries.text: The tiers of the Charms classroom were built for a professor who wished to see every wand in the room at once. She also wished every student to see her, and stood on a stack of books to make sure of it.

entries.title: The Apple Cellar
entries.text: Before it held cauldrons, the Potions classroom in the dungeons was the castle's cold store for apples. On damp days some students still claim they can smell them, under everything else.

entries.title: The Trophy Stair
entries.text: The Trophy Stair was built to show off the castle's awards to visitors. Over time the visitors stopped coming and the trophies kept arriving, so now the stair is mostly polished by students serving detention.

entries.title: The Nameless Statues
entries.text: Four robed statues stand in the niches of the Long Gallery. Nobody knows who they portray. Each year the students give them new names, and each year at least one of the names is rude.

entries.title: The Rose Window
entries.text: The great round window at the east end of the Long Gallery was set so that on midsummer morning it throws a perfect rose of coloured light onto the gallery floor. Students who stand in the middle of it are said to forget their homework.

entries.title: The Founding of the Dueling Club
entries.text: The Dueling Club was founded by two friends who could not stop arguing. They agreed to settle every argument by a formal duel, with a bow before and a bow after. Their arguments never ended, but their manners became famous.

entries.title: The Fires That Never Go Out
entries.text: The hearths of the four common rooms have not gone out in living memory. No one tends them. On cold nights the fires burn higher on their own, and on warm ones they settle to a polite glow.

entries.title: Madder, Weld and Woad
entries.text: The castle once grew its own dye plants in the kitchen gardens: madder for red, weld for yellow and woad for blue. Every robe in the castle was dyed in great vats by the lake, which turned the shallows purple for a week each summer.

entries.title: The Moonflower
entries.text: The moonflower opens only at night and closes again at the first light. Astronomy students once harvested the petals by starlight between lessons, for brews that were never quite the same when made by day.

entries.title: The Old Star Charts
entries.text: The star charts kept in the Astronomy Tower name constellations used nowhere else: the Lantern, the Heron, the Kettle, the Sleeping Hound and the Owl. Whoever drew them first is unknown, but they drew the Kettle with great affection.

entries.title: Ninety-Nine Cups
entries.text: The teacups of the Divination room are said to come from a single service of ninety-nine cups. One cup was broken long ago, and the professors still set out ninety-nine saucers, in case it comes back.

entries.title: The First Notice Board
entries.text: There was once a single notice board, in the Entrance Hall. Students pinned so many notes to it that it fell over one night with a sound like thunder. The next morning each common room had a board of its own.

entries.title: The Owls' Strike of 1803
entries.text: In 1803 the castle owls refused to fly for three whole days. The post piled up in the Entrance Hall until somebody noticed that the perches in the tower were rotten. The perches were mended, and the post resumed at once.

entries.title: The Great Snow of 1690
entries.text: In the winter of 1690 the snow fell so deep that the great doors of the Entrance Hall had to be dug out from the inside. The students built a snow castle on the lawn, complete with moving stairs, which collapsed by teatime.

entries.title: The Clock That Ran Backward
entries.text: For one week in spring, the clock in the Entrance Hall ran backward. Lessons were not affected, but several students claimed they had handed in their essays before writing them. The clock has behaved itself since.

entries.title: The Library's First Rule
entries.text: The first rule of the library, carved above its door in the old style, asks readers to speak only in whispers. It was carved by a librarian who had a very loud voice, and is said to have been a note to herself.

entries.title: The First Glasshouse
entries.text: The first greenhouse on the grounds was a single pane of glass propped against the kitchen garden wall, built to keep one homesick lemon tree alive through the winter. The tree survived. The glasshouses grew around it, pane by pane, for two hundred years.

entries.title: The Lemon Tree's Heirs
entries.text: No lemon tree stands in the greenhouses now, but every spring one bench is left empty and swept, with a watering can beside it. The gardeners say it is out of respect. The students say it is in case the tree comes back for its can.

entries.title: Why the Gnashvine Bites
entries.text: The Gnashvine was bred to guard seed trays from mice. It worked very well on the mice, and rather too well on the gardeners. A gardener named Petronel Ashby taught the vine to tell a mouse from a sleeve by keeping her sleeves rolled up for eleven years.

entries.title: The Shriekroot Rota
entries.text: When the castle grew its first Shriekroots, the gardeners drew up a rota so that only one person at a time had to hear them. The rota hung in the potting shed for a century, and the name at the top of it was crossed out four hundred and twelve times.

entries.title: Earmuffs for Everyone
entries.text: The greenhouse earmuffs were knitted one winter by the Burrowsby students as a gift to the gardeners. They knitted so many that there were earmuffs left over for the owls, the portraits and one very surprised suit of armour.

entries.title: The Needlebriar Hedge
entries.text: A Needlebriar hedge once ran the length of the kitchen garden, planted to keep the deer out of the cabbages. The deer stayed out. So did the cooks, the gardeners and anyone wanting cabbages, and the hedge was moved to a pot the following year.

entries.title: The Fern That Hid
entries.text: The Shiverfern curls up at the first unkind word. A professor once lost a whole tray of them during an argument about watering and found them a week later, tightly curled, under the bench. The professors have spoken gently in the greenhouses ever since.

entries.title: Rain Barrels of the West Wall
entries.text: Along the west wall of the greenhouses stand nine rain barrels, each fed by its own gutter. The gardeners claim that the rain in each barrel tastes different, and that the third barrel is the only one fit for ferns.

entries.title: The Elder by the Gate
entries.text: An old elder tree grows by the path to the greenhouses. Its berries were once pressed for the castle's purple dye, and the stains on the path stones are said to be three centuries deep. Students are asked not to try scrubbing them.

entries.title: The Rose Hip Harvest
entries.text: Each autumn the castle's wild roses were stripped of their hips for syrup and dye. The students who gathered the most were excused from one essay, a custom that ended when someone gathered nine sacks and asked to be excused from all of them.

entries.title: Glowcaps in the Cold Frames
entries.text: The glowing mushrooms were first found growing in a forgotten cold frame behind the greenhouses, lighting it up like a lantern. The gardener who found them moved them inside, and the cold frame has been dark and sulking ever since.

entries.title: The Potting Shed Clock
entries.text: The potting shed has a clock that runs to the plants' time rather than the castle's. It is slow in winter and quick in spring, and it stops altogether for a day each autumn while the leaves turn. Nobody uses it to be on time for anything.

entries.title: Gardener Ashby's Rules
entries.text: Petronel Ashby left three rules for the greenhouses, painted on a board by the door: water before you speak, never turn your back on a vine, and always wipe your shears. A fourth rule was added later by another hand: listen to rule two.

entries.title: The Paddock Before the Paddock
entries.text: Before there was a creature paddock, the castle's animals lived wherever they liked, which was mostly the kitchens. The paddock was fenced in after a Lynxkit was found asleep in a pudding basin on the morning of a feast.

entries.title: The Paddock Fence
entries.text: The paddock's fence was built low on purpose, low enough for a student to lean on and talk to whatever is on the other side. The builder believed that creatures learn more from a conversation than from a cage, and the fence has never been raised.

entries.title: The First Fluffbells
entries.text: The castle's first Fluffbells arrived in a hatbox, sent by a family who had too many of them. The note inside said only: They are no trouble at all. By the end of the month there were twenty, and the hatbox had become a home for all of them.

entries.title: What Fluffbells Eat
entries.text: Fluffbells will eat almost anything left within reach of their long tongues, including crumbs, spiders and, on one recorded occasion, an entire Herbology essay. The student was given an extension, on condition that he did not try the excuse twice.

entries.title: Mistress Corrie's Lynxkit
entries.text: The first Lynxkit at the castle belonged to a housekeeper named Corrie Lunn. It followed her on her rounds and would stop at any door behind which someone was up to no good. Mistress Corrie never had to knock twice.

entries.title: Why Lynxkits Watch the Gate
entries.text: The paddock's Lynxkits always sit facing the gate. The keepers once believed they were waiting for visitors; the Lynxkits, if asked, would say they are counting who comes in, so that they know who to blame afterwards.

entries.title: The Hippogriff Feather Box
entries.text: In the paddock hut there is a box of hippogriff feathers, each one shed and gathered rather than plucked. A keeper long ago decided that a feather freely given flies truer as a quill, and the castle's best quills have come from the box ever since.

entries.title: The Bow at the Paddock Gate
entries.text: Visitors to the paddock are taught to bow at the gate. Some of the creatures do not mind either way, but the ones that do mind are very particular, and the custom costs nothing. The paddock keepers bow too, even when nobody is looking.

entries.title: The Keepers' Lantern
entries.text: A single lantern hangs over the paddock gate and is never put out. It was first lit by a keeper who wanted lost students to find their way back from the grounds at night, and every keeper since has trimmed its wick before going to bed.

entries.title: The Gatehouse Portcullis
entries.text: The portcullis over the courtyard gate has not been lowered in living memory. The chains were oiled for a hundred years in case it was needed, then oiled for another hundred out of habit. A pair of swallows now nests in the top of it.

entries.title: The Courtyard Fountain
entries.text: The fountain in the Entrance Courtyard was a gift from the first graduating class, who each added a coin to its basin for luck. The coins are still there. The basin is cleaned every spring, and every spring the coins are put carefully back.

entries.title: The Fountain's Three Tiers
entries.text: The courtyard fountain has three tiers because its builders could not agree on two or four. Water runs from the top tier to the bottom in a little under a minute, and students waiting for lessons have timed it so often that the time is known to the second.

entries.title: Market Days in the Exchange Yard
entries.text: The stalls in the Exchange Yard were first set up for a single market day each term, when students could buy and sell without going to the village. The market was so popular that the stalls were never taken down, and now every day is a market day.

entries.title: The Stall Awnings
entries.text: Each of the four market stalls in the Exchange Yard flies an awning in a house's colours. The awnings were stitched by the four houses together, each house sewing another house's awning, so that no house could complain about its own.

entries.title: The Lamp Posts of the Yard
entries.text: The lamp posts in the courtyard burn the same moonstone oil as the castle lamps. On the coldest nights the flames lean toward the castle doors, as if they too would rather be inside.

entries.title: The Grounds' First Path
entries.text: The path from the courtyard gate down to the lake was worn by students long before it was paved. The paving was laid exactly over the worn track, bends and all, because the builders could find no better way down than the one the students had already chosen.

entries.title: The Lake's Silver Morning
entries.text: On the first frost of each winter the whole surface of the lake turns silver for an hour after sunrise. Students who are awake to see it are said to write good letters home that week. Students who are not awake are said to sleep very well.

entries.title: The Night Lessons
entries.text: Lessons after midnight began with Astronomy, which could not be taught any other way. Other professors soon found that some subjects suit the dark: the night-flowering plants, the creatures that wake at dusk, and students too tired to argue.

entries.title: The Midnight Bench
entries.text: One bench in the greenhouses is kept for plants that wake only at night. It is fitted with blinds that close at sunrise. Students working there are asked to whisper, not for the plants' sake, but because the day plants are trying to sleep.

entries.title: The Timetable Board
entries.text: The first timetable of the school was painted on a board in the Entrance Hall and repainted every term. One term the painter ran out of room and squeezed the last lesson onto the frame. That lesson was Herbology, and the gardeners have never let anyone forget it.

entries.title: Eighteen Bells
entries.text: In the oldest timetables each lesson began with a bell, and there were eighteen bells in a day. The bell ringer complained that the castle had more lessons than hours, and was given an apprentice, who complained about the same thing.

entries.title: The Absent Professor's Chair
entries.text: In each classroom there was once a spare chair for a professor who might arrive late. The chairs stayed long after anyone remembered why. A few still stand in corners, and students who sit in them are said to be asked the hardest question of the day.

entries.title: The Tide of Owls
entries.text: Every morning the castle owls leave together and return together, in a great grey wave over the courtyard. On days when one owl comes back late, the others wait on the gatehouse until it arrives, then file into the tower in order.

entries.title: Bram Hollins's Hat
entries.text: The hat Bram Hollins wore while training the first castle owls was kept in the West Tower long after he retired. It was so scratched by talons that it looked like lace. When it finally fell apart, the owls lined their nests with it.

entries.title: The Quiet Corridor Rule
entries.text: On the fourth floor there is a corridor where students may not run. The rule was made after a professor carrying forty jars of pickled eels met a student carrying a cake. Nobody remembers who won, but everyone remembers the smell.

entries.title: The Kitchens' First Cook
entries.text: The castle's first cook was a woman called Maud Penlow, who cooked for three hundred on a hearth meant for thirty. She is remembered for a stew that could feed the whole castle and still, mysteriously, leave enough for seconds.

entries.title: Penlow's Pot
entries.text: Maud Penlow's great iron pot still hangs in the kitchens. It is too heavy to lift and too old to cook in, but every feast day a single spoonful of something is stirred in it for luck. Nobody has ever told the students what.

entries.title: The Barrel Stack
entries.text: The barrels outside one common room were first stacked there by a cellarman who was tired of rolling them back to the kitchens. A house moved in behind them and never left, and the cellarman's barrels have not been rolled anywhere since.

entries.title: The Common Room Rugs
entries.text: The rugs of the four common rooms were woven by the same family of weavers over three generations. Each generation added one row of pattern that no one else noticed. Students who find the three rows are said to have very good eyes, and very little homework.

entries.title: The Hearth Steps
entries.text: The hearth steps of the common rooms were meant for setting down kettles, not for sitting. Students sat on them anyway, and after a century the stone wore smooth in the shape of two hundred years of elbows.

entries.title: The Lost Wing
entries.text: There is said to be a wing of the castle that was built, furnished and then forgotten. The plans show it clearly. The castle does not. Every few years a student claims to have found the door, and every few years the door is a cupboard.

entries.title: The Charmed Inkwells
entries.text: The inkwells in the oldest classrooms refill themselves at midnight. A professor charmed them to save time, and forgot to tell the kitchen staff, who went on filling them by hand for twenty years. The desks are still stained blue.

entries.title: The Inkwell Tax
entries.text: When the inkwells began refilling themselves, the castle's ink supplier wrote a stern letter asking for compensation. The headmaster sent him a single quill in reply. The supplier framed it, and the letter is the only thing on record he ever lost.

entries.title: The Divination Ladder's Rungs
entries.text: The ladder to the Divination room has thirteen rungs. Students counting on the way up often make it twelve or fourteen. The professors say the ladder adjusts itself to how ready a student is to learn. The caretakers say it needs fixing.

entries.title: The Crystal of the Tower Room
entries.text: The great crystal ball in the Divination room was carried up the ladder by six students on a winter evening. It took them three hours. The professor who ordered it said she had foreseen it would take two, and gave them all extra marks for patience.

entries.title: The Star Chart Copyists
entries.text: The Astronomy Tower's star charts have been copied so many times that every copy differs a little. In one copy the Sleeping Hound has a second tail, and in another the Heron wears a hat. The professors keep both, in case the sky changes its mind.

entries.title: The Telescope Lending Book
entries.text: The telescopes of the Astronomy Tower are lent out from a book kept by the door. The book is older than any of the telescopes, and its first entry records a borrowed telescope that was never returned. A note beside it reads: still looking.

entries.title: The Dueling Club's Bow
entries.text: The bow before a duel in the club is a deep one, and the bow after is deeper. The custom grew from the club's founders, who held that the winner owed the loser a lesson and the loser owed the winner a better duel next time.

entries.title: The House Cup Tankard's Successor
entries.text: After the pewter tankard was retired, the House Cup became a silver bowl, then a glass goblet, then the hourglasses that stand in the Great Hall. The prefects say the hourglasses are the best of them, because nobody can drink from an hourglass.

entries.title: The Pennant Makers
entries.text: The pennants given to the winners of the House Cup were first sewn by the losing houses, as a gesture of good grace. The custom did not last. The stitches grew steadily smaller and steadily less gracious, until the castle took the sewing over.

entries.title: The Castle's Last Word
entries.text: Old students say the castle always has the last word. Doors close a moment after you pass, stairs settle after you climb, and lamps dim once you are asleep. The castle is said to be listening, and, on the whole, to approve.
